item.title: Raji Doshi, 12, designed an algae system to reduce ocean acidity; now eyes $25,000 science prize
item.description: A young student from Connecticut is a finalist in a science competition for her innovative project. Her project proposes using algae and natural calcium buffers to reduce ocean acidification. This innovative idea could help protect vulnerable marine organisms from acidic conditions. She is competing for a substantial grand prize and valuable scientific mentorship. Her work highlights the significant contributions young minds can make to environmental solutions.

item.title: Meet the General Grant Tree: The world's second-largest tree that became America's only living National Shrine
item.description: The General Grant Tree stands as the world's second-largest tree by volume. It became America's National Christmas Tree in nineteen twenty-six. President Dwight D. Eisenhower declared it a living National Shrine in nineteen fifty-six. This sequoia honors men and women who served the nation. Its size and history make it a remarkable natural landmark.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Pacific trend raised US Southwest wildfire area 22%, cut Australia’s 19%
item.description: A Pacific Ocean warming trend has impacted wildfire conditions globally. This pattern amplified fire risks in the southwestern United States significantly. Conversely, it eased fire conditions in eastern Australia during the study. Researchers analyzed decades of wildfire and climate data for these findings. Understanding these ocean-climate links can improve future wildfire forecasts.

item.title: Nearly 81 years after Hiroshima, scientists discover a hidden metal alloy created by the atomic bomb blast
item.description: Scientists found a new metallic alloy in Hiroshima shoreline sand. This alloy formed from extreme heat and rapid cooling during the 1945 atomic blast. Researchers identified its unique chemical makeup and crystal structure in microscopic particles. The discovery offers insights into matter behavior under extreme conditions. This finding could inspire future materials science research and nuclear forensics.

item.title: Celebrities who were practising doctors before they became famous
item.description: Many doctors have pursued alternative careers, finding success in creative fields. Michael Crichton became a renowned author and screenwriter after medical school. Ken Jeong transitioned from internal medicine to a popular acting career. Khaled Hosseini became a best-selling author after practicing medicine. Che Guevara and Sir Arthur Conan Doyle also left medicine for significant impact.

item.title: Fans Split Over Self-Mural: Clavicular penthouse photo sparks debate; critics see dictator narcissism, others defend art
item.description: Clavicular sparked a social media storm after a photo of a massive self-portrait mural inside his penthouse went viral. Many fans mocked the artwork, comparing it to a dictator-style portrait, while others defended it as an impressive artistic choice. The online debate quickly filled with jokes, criticism, and praise, turning the mural into a trending topic and leaving social media sharply divided over its meaning and symbolism.

item.title: Charlie Kirk Assassination Case: Candace Owens questions FBI timeline; casts doubt on evidence
item.description: Candace Owens has questioned the FBI's response timeline in the Charlie Kirk murder investigation, asking why agents arrived at Utah Valley University so quickly. She also challenged key parts of the prosecution's case against Tyler Robinson, including the evidence presented and the official account of the shooting, while continuing to raise doubts about the federal investigation.

item.title: Quote of the day by Cicero: 'If we are not ashamed to think it, we should not be ashamed to say it'
item.description: Cicero, the Roman statesman, passionately argued for the alignment of one's thoughts with spoken words, critiquing the harmful effects of self-censorship. He posited that institutions become vulnerable when necessary truths go unspoken, a lesson still applicable in today's workplaces and government. The consequences of silence can be dire, stifling effective problem-solving. Open dialogue is essential for maintaining integrity and avoiding misguided decisions.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Quote of the day by Homer: 'Of all creatures that breathe and move upon the earth, nothing is...'
item.description: Homer's Odyssey explores the delicate balance of human existence, revealing how unpredictability shapes our lives. The ancient Greeks regarded people as ephemeroi—fleeting beings, a stark contrast to the enduring gods. This perspective remains significant today, as seen in the volatility of financial markets and professional sports, where fortunes fluctuate rapidly. Embracing our vulnerabilities can lead to humility and more effective planning.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: US scientists analysed 55 storm and atmospheric variables to identify hurricane rapid intensification
item.description: Coastal communities might soon benefit from enhanced hurricane forecasting. A groundbreaking statistical model predicts rapid hurricane intensification up to five days in advance, significantly improving early warnings. This innovation analyzes a multitude of environmental factors, allowing forecasters to anticipate dangerous storm developments with increased accuracy, ultimately safeguarding lives and property from unexpected hurricane threats.

item.title: Hungary shut its only nuclear plant for the first time in 44 years
item.description: Hungary's sole nuclear facility has been offline due to unprecedentedly low levels of the Danube River. This shutdown exacerbates power shortages amid a fierce summer heatwave, prompting the government to urge both households and businesses to conserve energy. Consequently, Hungary must depend on costly electricity imports from neighboring countries, highlighting the fragility of energy systems in the face of severe weather changes.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: 9,000 discarded Christmas trees help restore New Orleans wetlands
item.description: New Orleans is giving used Christmas trees a second life by dropping them into coastal marshes to help slow land loss. The bundled trees trap sediment, reduce wave energy and support marsh grass growth. Scientists say the method helps restore wetlands in selected areas but is only one part of Louisiana's broader coastal protection efforts.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Ex-nurse revives baby who stopped breathing during Arizona post-office visit
item.description: A former nurse's quick actions saved an infant's life at an Arizona post office. Mary Schwarz performed CPR and airway clearing on baby Nova who stopped breathing. Police Lieutenant Shari Aguilar then transported the infant to a nearby clinic for immediate medical attention. Nova, who had prior heart issues, began breathing again during the car ride. This incident highlights the critical importance of CPR training in everyday situations.
